questions.question: Illustrate how the MGNREGP strengthens livelihood security in rural India.
questions.solution_html:
• Illustrate how the MGNREGP strengthens livelihood security in rural India.
  •  Employment guarantee: Provides 100 days of paid manual work per year to rural households,
  • ensuring minimum income security.
  •  Asset creation: Builds rural infrastructure such as roads, ponds, and irrigation facilities, enhancing
  • long-term productivity.
  •  Empowerment and inclusion: Promotes women’s participation and reduces distress migration by
  • offering local employment.
  • /[CO7]

questions.question: Identify key features of traditional economic systems.
questions.solution_html:
• Identify key features of traditional economic systems.
  •  Subsistence production: Focus on meeting local and family needs rather than profit-making.
  •  Custom-based exchange: Economic roles and trade governed by traditions, norms, and bartering.
  •  Limited technological change: Slow adoption of innovation and dependence on natural resources.
  • /[CO1]

questions.question: Evaluate the usefulness of the Palma Ratio compared to other inequality measures in assessing income distribution.
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the usefulness of the Palma Ratio compared to other inequality measures in assessing income
  • distribution.
  •  Focus on extremes: Compares the income share of the top 10% to the bottom 40%, highlighting
  • inequality more clearly.
  •  Policy relevance: Easier for policymakers to target redistribution toward the poorest groups.
  •  Improvement over Gini: More intuitive and less sensitive to middle-income changes than the Gini
  • coefficient.
  • /[CO3]

questions.question: Demonstrate with examples how growth models can be critiqued
questions.solution_html:
• Demonstrate with examples how growth models can be critiqued
  • a. Neglect of inequality: Models like Rostow’s stages emphasize GDP growth but ignore social
  • disparities.
  • b. Environmental concerns: Growth-centric models overlook sustainability, as seen in
  • industrialization-driven pollution.
  • c. Cultural bias: Western models may not suit local contexts (e.g., dependency theory critique of
  • modernization).
  • d. Overreliance on markets: Neoliberal models assume trickle-down benefits that rarely reach the
  • poor.
  • e. Alternative perspectives: Human Development Index (HDI) and Sustainable Development Goals
  • (SDGs) focus on wellbeing, not just growth.
  • /[CO2]

questions.question: Discuss the interaction between health and economic poverty traps. [5x3 = 15] Part D Essay Each question carries 15 marks
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the interaction between health and economic poverty traps.
  • a. Poor health reduces productivity: Illness limits ability to work and earn income.
  • b. High medical costs: Out-of-pocket expenses push families deeper into poverty.
  • c. Malnutrition and low education: Weak health affects learning and long-term earning capacity.
  • d. Limited healthcare access: Rural and poor populations lack affordable medical services.
  • e. Cycle of deprivation: Poor health causes poverty, and poverty worsens health—creating a self-
  • reinforcing trap.
  • /[CO3]
